subject: Handshake plan: secure zipper for private deploys — peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S
messages:
From: Alice Vega <alice.vega@northshore.health>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Cc: network-ops@northshore.health
Date: 2026-08-20 15:03:00 +0000
Subject: Pilot connectivity — quick guidance requested

Hi team,

Thanks again for the onboarding call earlier. As we discussed, Northshore is preparing a 6-week pilot to validate a Redwood Private deployment inside our AWS tenancy. Two constraints to call out up front:

- Latency sensitivity for inference requests (90th percentile target <50ms to our app tier)
- Strict allowlist model: we can only open egress to a small set of private endpoints (security team requirement) and need source-IP preservation for token-based rate-limiting on our side

Options on the table from our engineering group: VPC peering (cross-account peering), PrivateLink (interface endpoint backed by a service in Redwood account), or a site-to-site IPsec VPN into our VPC. We need a short, pragmatic recommendation for the pilot that balances security, operational overhead, and latency.

Specific questions:
1) Given our need for source-IP preservation for rate limiting, which pattern preserves client source IP easiest?
2) Any throughput or burst limitations we should worry about for PrivateLink?
3) If we pick PrivateLink as primary, what minimal fallback do you recommend for off-hours bulk transfers?

I attached the pilot scope and a simple network sketch. Can you reply with a recommended path and a one-page mutual action plan (who does what, in what order)?

Thanks,
Alice
Alice Vega
Head of Engineering — Northshore Health
Attachment: northshore-pilot-scope.pdf (doc)
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Alice Vega <alice.vega@northshore.health>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-20 20:12:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Pilot connectivity — quick guidance requested

Alice — thanks for the clear constraints. Below is a short, pragmatic take (TL;DR up front, details after).

TL;DR recommendation:
- Primary: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) for inference traffic (lowest surface area, good security posture)
- Fallback for large batch transfers: short-lived site-to-site IPsec tunnel (VPN) or customer-managed S3 transfer over peering where large data movement is needed

Why PrivateLink as primary:
- Minimal routing exposure: it exposes a service endpoint rather than peering your entire VPC routing table to ours
- Security: you get an ENI in your VPC, traffic stays on AWS private fabric (no public internet hops)
- IAM + SG controls: you can gate source SGs and use VPC endpoint policies to restrict access

Tradeoffs & things to watch:
- Source IP preservation: classic PrivateLink interface endpoints terminate at the ENI in your VPC; the original client source IP is not always preserved to the backend because of how ENI/elastic network interfaces and AWS-managed proxies behave. If you need the original client IP for rate-limiting, we can preserve a client identifier in a TLS-mutual header or use a proxy that forwards X-Forwarded-For, but you should treat that as an application-level signal (not raw TCP source IP).
- VPC peering preserves source IPs across the peering link, but it opens up cross-account routing and increases blast radius. Suitable if you trust full network-level access and want exact source-IP behavior.
- S2S VPN preserves IP visibility but brings higher latency and more operational upkeep (IPSec tunnels, rekeys, monitoring). Good as a resilient fallback and for bulk data sync where latency is less critical.
- Throughput: PrivateLink scales but each ENI has limits; for heavy bulk transfers (multi-GB transfers), peering or a temporary Direct Connect/transfer path may be cheaper/faster. For small to medium inference traffic, PrivateLink is fine.

Suggested pilot handshake (order of operations):
1) Provision PrivateLink endpoint in Northshore test VPC (you) + create service-network mapping in Redwood (us)
2) Exchange endpoint permissions and test mutual TLS if you want connection-level auth
3) Validate end-to-end latency with a synthetic load test (we can provide a small harness)
4) If you hit bulk transfer needs, bring up an ephemeral S2S VPN between our pilot tenant and your data-transfer VPC, run sync, then tear down (minimizes standing ops)

Action items (quick):
- Alice: create a test subnet and open required SGs to allow interface ENI insertion (target by 2026-08-23)
- Kimberly: we'll prepare the PrivateLink service and prescriptive SG/policy template (done by 2026-08-22)
- Marissa: coordinate procurement path for any endpoint hours / reserved bandwidth if needed (will surface cost)

Attachments: architecture sketch (northshore_handshake_diagram.png), ops checklist (ops-risk-checklist.xlsx)

Notes on auditability: we can ship access logs and per-request metadata to your CloudWatch/Log destination for audit trails. If you require HSM-backed signing or KMS segregation, we should loop security early.

Happy to hop on a 30-min design call tomorrow to walk through the diagram.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Head, Customer Infra — Redwood Inference
Attachment: northshore_handshake_diagram.png (image), ops-risk-checklist.xlsx (spreadsheet)
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: Alice Vega <alice.vega@northshore.health>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-21 09:05:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Pilot connectivity — quick guidance requested

Karthik + Alice — a couple of operational-first concerns to flag before we lock on PrivateLink as primary: 

1) NAT & source-IP nuance: as Karthik called out, PrivateLink often requires us to run a load balancer/proxy behind the service which will typically source traffic from a small set of worker IPs. If Northshore's rate-limiter strictly requires the original client IP at the TCP layer, PrivateLink will need an app-level header workaround or VPC peering. Can your rate-limiter accept a signed header (we can HMAC a request ID) or a mutual TLS client cert?

2) Throughput and bursting: for inference request patterns (many small requests) PrivateLink is fine. For model checkpoint transfers or multi-GB artifacts, plan to use a temporary peering or S2S link — PrivateLink ENIs are not optimized for long-lived, very-high-throughput bulk transfers.

3) Monitoring & troubleshooting: operationally it's easier for your NetOps team if we publish a short runbook (connectivity checks, how to map ENI IDs to sessions, common failure modes). I attached a quick checklist.

If you prefer exact source-IP preservation and can tolerate slightly more surface area, peering may be the least-surprising from a network perspective. My vote for pilot: PrivateLink for inference calls + ephemeral S2S for bulk/data ops.

Kimberly Park
Principal Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
Attachment: ops-runbook-snippet.txt (text)

Alice — echoing Karthik and Kim. Operational pattern below (mutual action plan + dates) so we can move the pilot contract and SOW forward: 

Mutual action plan (pilot):
- 2026-08-22: Redwood prepares PrivateLink service and SG/policy templates (owner: Kimberly)
- 2026-08-23: Northshore provisions test VPC/subnet and shares endpoint IDs (owner: Alice)
- 2026-08-24: Redwood and Northshore run E2E latency tests and exchange logs (owner: Karthik + Northshore NetOps)
- 2026-08-25: If bulk transfer required, stand up ephemeral S2S for transfer window (owner: Northshore infra + Redwood infra)
- 2026-08-28: Pilot review and decision gate (continue with PrivateLink at scale or move to peering)

Commercial asks:
- We'll include a small line item for PrivateLink endpoint hours in the pilot SOW; Marissa to send a draft estimate by 2026-08-22.
- If Northshore requires peering instead, that will trigger a short security review and an SLA addendum.

If this plan looks good, I'll draft a one-page SOW and a brief decision checklist for the 08/28 review.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive — Redwood Inference
